entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Shaddād, known in ancient Arabian folklore as Shaddād bin ʽĀd, stands as a quintessential legendary tyrannical king whose narrative is deeply embedded in pre-Islamic Arabian tradition and later codified within Islamic texts. Though no historical records confirm his existence as a specific individual, his mythic persona represents an archetypal figure of immense power, hubris, and ultimate divine retribution. Shaddād is primarily significant as the fabled ruler of Iram of the Pillars, a lost city of immense wealth and architectural splendor, whose story serves as a cautionary tale illustrating the transience of worldly might against divine will, resonating across the Arabian Peninsula and beyond.

According to the narratives, Shaddād, a descendant of 'Ad al-Miltat ibn Saksak, inherited a vast kingdom and aspired to construct an earthly paradise to rival the heavens, specifically the Garden of Eden. This ambition manifested in the creation of Iram of the Pillars (often identified with Ubar), a city described as adorned with pillars of gold and silver, emeralds, and rubies, a testament to his unparalleled material wealth and architectural hubris. The Qur'an's Sura 89, "Al-Fajr" (The Dawn), alludes to the people of ʿĀd and Iram, stating, 'Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd – [with] Iram – who had lofty pillars, the likes of which had never been created in [any] land?' This scriptural mention cemented Shaddād's association with the city and his subsequent destruction for defying God, through a catastrophic wind that annihilated him and his people.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Shaddād holds significant regional importance as a central figure in Arabian folklore and Islamic tradition, influencing moral teachings and inspiring centuries of cultural narratives about hubris and divine justice. His legend shaped the perception of lost civilizations and served as an enduring cautionary tale across the Middle East.
